finding: §2 says the recommendation for the changed branch 'is decided here rather than left to an implementer', then decides a string for a branch it does not name. The trigger it names is 'the first clean round of a streak that still holds warning/info rows' — at audit_clean_rounds: 2 that round is not converged — but the text it decides ('states that the phase may proceed') is the converged branch's, and §7 row 10 pins only 'a converged round holding non-PASS rows'. Audit next_action has three branches (converged / open rows / clean-but-not-yet-converged); the branch §2 actually names ends the release with no decided text and no test row, so the implementer must invent the one sentence §2 says exists to stop an operator learning silently that a round closed over open rows.
suggestion: Give the exact recommendation for each of the two affected branches — clean-but-not-converged with non-PASS rows, and converged with non-PASS rows — and add a §7 row for the first.

finding: §3 calls the uncovering refusal 'an escalation rather than a deadlock' because 'the operator's resolution is to write the field explicitly into the imported document', but under the change rule that remedy works for only one of the two literals and §3 names neither. Writing `all` makes resolved-after equal resolved-before and passes — at the cost of the project-level `blocking` the operator deliberately set. Writing `blocking` changes the resolved value away from the task-level `all` and is refused by exactly the rule §3 states, and refused again on every retry, because the task override that would make resolved-before `blocking` is never written. So the stated resolution either abandons the field or does not lift the refusal, and an implementer cannot tell which import the fence is supposed to permit.
suggestion: Name the literal the operator writes and what happens on the retry. If an explicit `blocking` must be admitted once, state the mechanism (an attended import, an approved escalation, or a first-write exemption) instead of letting 'write the field explicitly' carry it.

finding: §3 specifies the fence as a comparison of resolved-before against resolved-after but never says a refused write leaves the tree unchanged. On `tp set` that is harmless; on `tp import`, which replaces the whole task-level workflow block and the task array, resolved-after is knowable only after the document is parsed and the prospective block assembled, so the implementer must decide whether the refusal happens before any bytes are written, after a write plus rollback, or after a partial write. Rows 12 and 13b assert an exit code and nothing about file state, so all three implementations pass.
suggestion: State that a fenced refusal is a no-op — exit 2 before any file is written — and assert it in rows 12 and 13b (the task file and .tp/config.json are byte-identical after the refusal).

finding: Three surfaces must classify a row's severity identically and the spec names a shared mechanism for none of them: record-time stamping (§2), the replay's per-round grading (row 11), and `--merge`'s buckets (row 17, whose invariant is that `error` + `unrecognised` equals the round's blocking-row count). §2 also forbids grading at read time, so the replay needs a pure grader the runtime does not otherwise expose, and §4 says the merge path has no access to the resolved policy at all. §7's own second paragraph says a row depending on a function states it; rows 5-8, 11 and 17 name none, so three independent classifications can drift while every row stays green.
suggestion: Name one predicate over (rows, resolved policy) and state that stamping, the replay and the merge buckets all derive from it, so row 17's invariant cannot drift from §2's rule.

finding: Row 11 depends on a committed projection whose path, schema and derivation the spec never gives — only a size (~295 KiB), a provenance ('committed with the commit it was taken from') and the four fields it keeps. An implementer must invent a location, a row format and a regeneration procedure, and no later reader can check that the fixture is still the projection of the corpus it claims, which is the only thing making row 11's four numbers falsifiable. §7's own paragraph two states that a row depending on a file now states it.
suggestion: Name the fixture path, its per-row schema, the command that regenerates it from spec/.tp-review/, and how the source commit is recorded so a drifted fixture is detectable.

finding: §6a's heading and framing say five shipped assertions are *reversed*; row 18 requires the eleven `assert.`/`require.` sites in TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate to become nine and the nine to be 'the ones that do not name `audit_converge_on`' — that is deletion. A genuinely reversed assertion (the field IS a known workflow field) keeps the count at eleven and still names the field, failing row 18 on both clauses. The spec never says which is wanted, and under the deletion reading the gate guard ends this release asserting strictly less than it does today, with no row taking over the positive statement.
suggestion: Say explicitly that the two sites are removed, and either add a row asserting the field is now a legal workflow field at that guard, or state why the guard should no longer carry it.

finding: Row 19 prescribes the replacement clause for both doc sentences — audit convergence counts every non-`PASS` row 'whose severity the resolved policy treats as blocking'. §2 defines blocking severity as `error` (plus unrecognised) with no policy relativity, and under `all` cleanliness does not consult severity at all: every non-`PASS` row counts whatever its severity. Read with §2's definition the replacement is false under the default (it implies warning and info rows do not count); read as policy-relative it uses 'blocking' in a sense §2 never defines. §6a's closing line claims each replacement is true under both values, so the implementer cannot ship the prescribed literal and satisfy §6a at the same time.
suggestion: Either define in §2 what 'the resolved policy treats as blocking' means under `all` (every severity), or give a replacement sentence that names both policies explicitly.

finding: §2 requires next_action to name 'how many non-`PASS` rows were accepted' and row 10 requires that numeral on both audit sinks, but the population is never named. Three candidates in this same release disagree: the latest recorded round's non-`PASS` row total, the sum of `role_streaks[].open` (which §4 calls severity-blind and unconditional on both sinks), and `--merge`'s `findings`. They differ whenever a row carries no role or a role contributes no rows to the latest round, and only the second is already available to `--status` without re-reading the round file.
suggestion: Name the population — the non-`PASS` rows of the latest recorded round — and say whether it is recomputed or read from an already-emitted field, so both sinks provably print the same number.

finding: §3 declares the write paths to be three (`tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, `tp import`) while row 4 makes `tp config --extract` field-aware — a fourth command that writes `audit_converge_on` into `.tp/config.json`. Whether extract needs the fence is never stated. If the fence is built as three per-command patches, which §3's enumeration invites, extract ships unfenced; if it is built at the resolution layer, extract is covered and the enumeration is misleading about the design. The safety argument (extract hoists only a value common to every task file, so nothing it writes can change what resolves for them) is derivable but appears nowhere, so the implementer re-derives it or guesses.
suggestion: State whether the fence is a rule at the resolution layer or a set of per-command checks, and record extract's exemption with its reason — or add it to the fenced list.

finding: §3 says the release 'adds `audit-converge-on` to that enum, maps the field to it, and refuses with a message', which reads as a refusal naming a decision the unit then escalates with; row 14 says 'a fenced refusal **records** `--decision audit-converge-on`'. Those are different builds — the refusing command writing the run's escalation record itself, versus exiting 2 with a message the unit acts on by calling `tp escalate` — and they differ in whether a run reaches `stop_reason: escalation` without the unit cooperating, in what the exit code means, and in what row 14 can observe.
suggestion: Say which actor writes the escalation record, and restate row 14's assertion against that actor's observable.

finding: Row 20 requires REFERENCE.md's 'Honest Convergence Signals' paragraph to stop listing the stored per-round `clean` flag, and its own mutant column concedes that leaving it is something 'the guard does not currently catch'. So the row names an assertion with no enforcing mechanism: the release must extend the docs-contract guard over that paragraph — new work the spec does not describe, with no anchor phrase or literal given — or accept a one-time edit no test protects. §6a items 2 and 3 are explicitly pinned by a named guard and item 4 is not, and the difference is never acknowledged.
suggestion: State what the guard asserts over that paragraph (an anchor phrase, or the absence of the `clean` mention), or mark item 4 as a deliberately unguarded edit and say why that is acceptable.

finding: §4 says every row lands in a named bucket but never says whether `by_severity` always carries all four keys (zeros included) or only the buckets that are non-empty. The two counters it is explicitly modelled on, `by_status` and `by_role`, carry only observed keys, so the natural implementation omits `error` on an advisory-only round — exactly the round §4 exists for. Row 17's invariant is written as a sum over keys that may then be absent, and an agent reading `by_severity.error` to decide whether the round blocks must know whether absent means zero or means unknown.
suggestion: State that all four keys are present with explicit zeros whenever the object is emitted (or that absent means zero), and assert that in row 17.

finding: `tp audit --merge` deduplicates rows and reports `duplicates_removed`; §4 says the new counter goes in the loop that builds `by_status` and `by_role` but never says whether `by_severity` counts the deduplicated set or the raw inputs. Row 17 ties `error` + `unrecognised` to 'the round's blocking-row count', which is the deduplicated population only if the counter runs after dedup — under the other reading a duplicated `error` row inflates the blocking count that §2's fail-closed rule is supposed to mirror.
suggestion: State that `by_severity` counts the merged (deduplicated) rows, the same population as `by_status`, and say so in row 17's assertion.

finding: §2 says an invalid value is refused at 'the consuming sink' and row 3 names only `tp audit --record` and `--status`. The other readers of the resolved workflow are unaddressed: the plain prompt-emitting `tp audit <spec>`, which prints the loop budget; `tp resume` / `tp run`'s oracle; and `tp config --resolved`. The implementer must decide whether those refuse, ignore the value, or fall back to `all` — and a silent fallback at one reader while another exits ExitValidation gives two answers about the same stored file, which is the failure mode fail-closed grading exists to avoid.
suggestion: Name every reader that validates, or state a single resolution point that validates once so all readers inherit the refusal.

finding: §2.1 makes a documented one-line command a deliverable — the command deriving the previous cycle's severity mix from `audit-round-*.ndjson`, which §2.1 calls the stated basis for the whole decision — without giving the command, the directory it runs over, or what it prints. §7 carries no row for it, so the single artifact §2.1 says an operator needs at decision time is both unspecified and unverified, while §7 claims every row derives from a numbered decision.
suggestion: Give the command verbatim in §2.1 and add a §7 row asserting SKILL.md carries it beside the field's documentation.

finding: §3 scopes the fence to `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and row 13c tests the variable unset; everything in between is unspecified — `TP_UNATTENDED=0`, `TP_UNATTENDED=true`, or set-but-empty. An implementer choosing `value == "1"` and one choosing 'set and non-empty' both satisfy §3 and row 13c while disagreeing about whether the fence applies, and the disagreement runs in the unsafe direction for any runner that exports a different truthy value.
suggestion: State the predicate once — which values count as unattended — and have row 13c assert the boundary rather than only the unset case.

finding: 'the same terms and with the same hint as `review_converge_on`' delegates the user-visible message to a string the spec neither quotes nor constrains. Row 3 asserts exit codes only, so any hint passes — including one copied verbatim from the review field, which would name review's severity vocabulary that §2 says explicitly does not apply to audit rows.
suggestion: Quote the hint, or state the property it must have: it names this field, its two literals, and no review severity.
